Validate the following vignette.

Patient demographics:
  age: 66
  gender: Male
  ethnicity: European
  relationship_status: Married
  occupation: Software Engineer
  trauma_type: Physical abuse by caregiver (childhood)
  pcl5: 33

Patient-reported symptoms:
  Triggers: Tactile (Temperature): A specific temperature on the skin, Somatic (Heart Racing): Own heart racing or pounding, Intrusive Memory: A memory of the event coming to mind suddenly
  Maladaptive Strategies: Avoid Own Body: Paying attention to or looking at my own body, Avoid Social Contacts: Seeing people that I socialised with before the event, Avoid Being Touched: Any form of physical contact with others
  Threat: Noticing Weapons: I notice potential weapons or dangerous objects in any environment, Body Reacts Before Mind: My body reacts to danger before I have even had time to think, Startle to Touch: I react with alarm when someone touches me unexpectedly
  Negative Appraisals: Constant Vigilance: I have to be especially careful because you never know what can happen next, Outsider: I am permanently an outsider now, Mistrust: People can't be trusted

Vignette:
As a child, Hans had grown accustomed to the sound of his father's belt buckle being unfastened, signaling the start of another brutal beating. The memories of those events still lingered, and at 66 years old, Hans found himself constantly on edge, as if waiting for the next assault. It was not just the physical pain that haunted him but also the feeling of utter helplessness that came with being trapped in a situation he couldn't escape. One particular memory had become etched in his mind – the time his father had left him locked in the attic without food or water for an entire weekend. The temperature in the cramped space had been sweltering, and Hans recalled the sensation of sweat dripping down his face as he desperately tried to find a way out. To this day, whenever he felt a sudden rush of heat on his skin, he was instantly transported back to that attic, his heart racing with fear. As an adult, Hans struggled to make sense of these flashbacks and the subsequent anxiety they triggered. He had come to believe that if he could just avoid certain situations, he might be able to stave off the memories and the accompanying terror. For instance, he found it increasingly difficult to tolerate being touched by others, even his wife. The gentlest caress would send his body into overdrive, as if anticipating another brutal attack. Hans's aversion to physical contact had also led him to become withdrawn socially. He stopped attending gatherings with friends and acquaintances from before the traumatic events, fearing that they might notice something was amiss or, worse still, try to initiate conversation about his past. At work, he found himself preoccupied with potential threats, meticulously scanning his surroundings for objects that could be used as weapons. His colleagues began to comment on Hans's increasing paranoia and his tendency to startle at the slightest touch. They couldn't understand why someone so skilled in software engineering had become so detached from the team. What they didn't see was the constant inner struggle – the perpetual state of hypervigilance, always anticipating danger lurking around every corner. Hans felt like an outsider looking in, as if he no longer belonged in his own life. He couldn't shake off the feeling that people were watching him, waiting for him to slip up so they could pounce. His wife, though well-intentioned, only seemed to exacerbate this sense of mistrust with her innocent queries about his past. It wasn't until Hans's granddaughter began asking why he never wanted to play or hug her that the reality of his situation hit home. He didn't want to pass on his fears and anxieties to another generation; it was time to confront the demons he had been running from for so long. The prospect of seeking help both terrified and liberated him – a chance, perhaps, to rewrite the narrative that had defined his life for far too long. As Hans sat in his dimly lit study, surrounded by the comforting glow of computer screens and the hum of machinery, he felt an overwhelming sense of trepidation about what lay ahead. Would therapy be able to undo the damage of decades past? Or would it simply uncover more wounds, leaving him even more exposed? The uncertainty was daunting, but for the first time in his life, Hans felt ready to face whatever came next – even if it meant finally letting go of the armor that had both protected and imprisoned him.
